opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Funnels are one of my favorite ideas in robotics, and I think they're underappreciated.

The basic problem in manipulation is uncertainty everywhere. You don't know exactly where the object is. Your sensors are noisy, your camera calibration is a little off, and the robot's motors have some slop. Friction is notoriously hard to model; it changes with humidity, with dust, with how many times a part has been handled. So if your strategy depends on knowing everything precisely, it's going to fail in the real world.

A funnel is the perfect counterexample. When you pour flour into a jar through a funnel, you don't need to aim precisely. Anywhere within that wide mouth works, and the geometry does the work of collapsing all those possible starting positions into one output. It takes a large set of uncertain states and maps them to a small, known state, without any sensing at all.

That idea goes back a long way in robotics. Matt Mason and Mike Erdmann worked on what they called sensorless manipulation. My own PhD work was on orienting parts with a simple parallel-jaw gripper. I showed that for any polygonal part, there's a sequence of squeezes that will bring it into a unique final orientation regardless of how it started. The gripper never needs to look at the part. Each squeeze is like a funnel, collapsing the range of possible orientations, and if you chain the right ones together you get down to exactly one. Industrial engineers had been doing this intuitively for decades with vibratory bowl feeders, those little tracks and fences that knock parts into the right orientation as they go by.

What I like about the funnel framing is that it flips the usual question. Instead of asking "how do I perceive the world more precisely?", you ask "how do I design actions that make precision unnecessary?" Often the second question is much easier to solve and much more robust.

It's also relevant to the current excitement about deep learning and large models for robots. There's a tendency to think we just need more data and bigger networks and the robot will learn to handle everything. Learning is really powerful, and we use it heavily in our lab, for example in Dex-Net for grasping. But I think the best results come from combining learning with these physical insights. A compliant gripper, a well-chosen pushing motion, a fixture with a chamfered edge: these are funnels built into the hardware or the action, and they absorb a lot of uncertainty that the learned model would otherwise have to handle.

So I'd say funnels are a reminder that physics can be your friend. You don't always have to fight uncertainty with more computation. Sometimes you can design the interaction so the uncertainty simply doesn't matter.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a funnel’s geometry lets physical interactions guide objects from a wide range of starting positions into a smaller, known state without precise sensing.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the idea of funnels goes back to Matt Mason, who was my advisor's colleague at MIT and later at Carnegie Mellon, and it's really one of the most beautiful ideas in manipulation. The intuition is this: when you're dealing with a physical object, you never know exactly where it is. There's always some uncertainty in its position, its orientation, its shape, friction, all of that. The naive approach is to try to sense your way out of that uncertainty, to put more and more cameras and sensors on the robot so that you know the state precisely. But that's expensive and it never fully works.

A funnel is a different approach. You design the physical action so that the uncertainty collapses on its own. Think about an actual funnel in your kitchen. You pour liquid in anywhere across the wide mouth, and it comes out the narrow spout in the same place every time. The mechanics do the work. You don't need to know where each drop started.

In manipulation you can do the same thing. The classic example is a part feeder. Say you have a bunch of parts dumped on a tray in random orientations. If you tilt the tray and let them slide against a series of fences at specific angles, the parts will reorient themselves as they bump against the fences, and after a few of these they all end up in the same orientation. My own thesis work was on this with a parallel jaw gripper. If you just squeeze a polygonal part between two flat jaws, the part rotates into one of a small number of stable orientations. Do a sequence of squeezes at the right angles, and you can guarantee the part ends up in a single known orientation, with no sensing at all. I proved that for any polygon, such a sequence exists. That was kind of a surprising result at the time.

What I like about this framing is that it reverses the usual mindset. Instead of asking "how do I know more?", you ask "how do I act so that I don't need to know?" It's exploiting physics, compliance, gravity, contact, to do computation for you. And I think it's still deeply relevant today, even in the era of learning-based robotics. When we design grasps, we're looking for ones that are robust to small errors in pose, which is really a funnel in the space of possible positions. A good grasp has a wide basin of attraction. And a lot of what makes certain tasks hard, like peg-in-hole or threading a needle, is that the natural funnel is very narrow, so you either need extreme precision or you need to engineer the geometry, like a chamfer on the hole, to widen it.

So funnels are, to me, a way of thinking about uncertainty as something you shape rather than something you fight.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a physical funnel uses its mechanics to guide material from a wide mouth to a narrow spout, and connects that idea to manipulation actions that make uncertainty collapse through physics.

astra-6.text:
I think funnels are a useful way to think about how you can get reliable behavior without knowing the exact state of the world. Imagine dropping a small part into a funnel. You don’t have to position it precisely at the top. There’s a whole range of starting positions, and the shape of the funnel guides them toward the same outcome.

In manipulation, contact can do something similar. Suppose a robot is holding an object and there’s some uncertainty about its position. Rather than trying to measure that position ever more precisely, it can push the object against a flat surface. Now you’ve constrained its position in one direction. You might then push it into a corner, constraining another direction. The action itself reduces uncertainty.

The interesting thing is that contact, which often makes robotics difficult, becomes a resource. You’re using the environment to help you. And you can think about composing these operations: one funnel gets you into a set of states where the next funnel works, and that takes you closer to the goal. You don’t need every motion to be perfectly precise if the sequence is designed to bring a range of possible states to a reliable outcome.

r001.rationale: The response says that a funnel’s shape guides objects from a range of starting positions toward the same outcome, conveying uncertainty reduction through the funnel’s physical guidance.

sol-6.1.text:
A funnel is a way of thinking about how you can start with a range of possible states and, through an action, bring them into a smaller range. Imagine dropping a part into a physical funnel: you don’t have to position it very accurately at the top, because the geometry guides it toward the same place at the bottom.

In manipulation, we look for actions that have that property. If a robot is uncertain about the orientation of an object, it might push it against a wall. A whole range of initial orientations can end up with one edge aligned against that wall. You’ve reduced uncertainty through contact, rather than having to measure everything more precisely.

And then you can compose those actions. One action constrains the orientation, another constrains the position, and eventually you have the object in a state where you can reliably grasp it or assemble it. The interesting shift is that uncertainty isn’t just something you have to observe and calculate around. You can design actions that physically reduce it.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a physical funnel’s geometry guides a part toward the same place at the bottom despite imprecise placement, illustrating how physical guidance narrows uncertainty.
